A stringent regulator reviews the full evidence on quality, safety and effectiveness. For malaria medicines this is usually the European Medicines Agency (EMA) EU-M4all procedure (formerly Article 58), which covers medicines meant for use outside Europe. Every later step builds on this opinion. Health authority review status is generally not public, so this step changes only when a regulator or the manufacturer announces an outcome.
EMA, or another stringent regulator such as the US FDA
Preparing the full dossier, then waiting out the review.
A WHO expert group weighs clinical evidence and decides whether the medicine is included in WHO guidelines for malaria.
WHO Department of Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases (MNT) and its Guidelines Development Group
The group meets on its own calendar, so the timing is hard to predict.

A separate WHO check of quality and manufacturing, including factory inspections. Prequalification supports eligibility for purchase under the quality assurance and procurement policies of UN agencies and major funders such as the Global Fund; specific policies and exceptions may differ. Manufacturers are invited to apply through a WHO Expression of Interest (EOI).
Waiting for an invitation round, then for inspections.

Each country's own regulator licenses the medicine before it can be sold or used there, usually one country at a time. Regional routes, such as the African Medicines Agency and WHO's collaborative registration (about 90 working days), are intended to speed this up.
Going country by country, each with its own queue.
Ministries of Health include the medicine in national treatment guidelines. These decide what health workers prescribe and what the public sector buys.
Ministries of Health and national malaria programmes
National guideline committees meet rarely and follow their own schedules.

Public funders, such as the Global Fund, other donors and national governments, run tenders, agree reference prices and forecast demand. A medicine can be recommended, registered and in the guidelines and still be barely bought. This step covers public channels only: the figures shown are Global Fund-financed procurement. Private commercial channels are not included.
The Global Fund, other donors, UNICEF and national governments
Financing cycles. Global Fund grants, for example, run for three years.
Global Fund price and quality reporting
Supply from port to health facility, health-worker training, and pharmacovigilance once the medicine is in use.
Supply chain readiness and health-worker training.
Artemisinin-based combination therapy — the standard class of malaria treatments pairing an artemisinin derivative with a longer-acting partner drug.

Stringent Regulatory Authority — the older WHO term for an advanced regulator such as EMA or the US FDA. WHO is replacing it with WHO-Listed Authorities (WLA), regulators assessed against WHO's performance indicators; existing SRAs are treated as WHO-listed during the transition.
WHO-Listed Authority — a regulator assessed by WHO as operating at an advanced level.
EU-Medicines for all, formerly the Article 58 procedure — EMA's scientific opinion on high-priority medicines intended for markets outside the EU.
Guidelines Development Group — the WHO expert group that reviews evidence and formulates treatment recommendations.

WHO prequalification — the quality, safety and efficacy assessment whose outcome, a listing on the WHO prequalified-products list, supports eligibility under the quality assurance (QA) and procurement policies of UN agencies and major funders; specific policies and exceptions may differ.
Multiple first-line therapies — the deliberate, managed use of two or more effective ACTs in a population for treatment of uncomplicated malaria, either simultaneously or in rotation.
Expression of Interest — the WHO prequalification invitation list; a product must be on it before a PQ dossier can be assessed.

African Medicines Agency — the African Union's continental medicines agency, based in Kigali, set up to harmonise regulation across the member states that have ratified its treaty and to evaluate selected priority products. National regulators still grant marketing authorisation.
U.S. President's Malaria Initiative — a major bilateral funder and procurer of malaria commodities.
Medicines for Malaria Venture — product development partnership behind several antimalarials.
Price & Quality Reporting — the Global Fund database of procurement transactions (volumes and prices).
Good Manufacturing Practice — quality standard verified by inspection of manufacturing sites.

LAUNCH, funded by Unitaid, is a proof of concept for making the access pathway of new antimalarial medicines transparent. It brings public information on each medicine together in one place, from development and regulatory approval through WHO recommendation and prequalification to registration, policy, procurement and delivery in countries, so that partners can see where access is held up and act on it.

It starts with four medicines relevant to multiple first-line therapy (MFT) strategies, which use more than one first-line treatment in a population to reduce the risk of drug resistance. Two are already recommended by WHO but underused: artesunate–pyronaridine (ASPY) and dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (DHA–PPQ). Two are in late-stage development: ganaplacide–lumefantrine (GanLum) and artemether–lumefantrine–amodiaquine (ALAQ). Together they cover both halves of the pathway: approval for the medicines in development, and adoption and procurement for those already recommended.

Tracking a medicine here does not mean that LAUNCH or Unitaid endorses it or recommends it for any use. The dashboard reports where each medicine stands on the access pathway, not whether it should be used. For this proof of concept the scope is these four medicines; it may later expand to other medicines and malaria tools.

stageInfo.who: EMA, or another stringent regulator such as the US FDA
stageInfo.stall: Preparing the full dossier, then waiting out the review.

stageInfo.what: A WHO expert group weighs clinical evidence and decides whether the medicine is included in WHO guidelines for malaria.
stageInfo.who: WHO Department of Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases (MNT) and its Guidelines Development Group
stageInfo.stall: The group meets on its own calendar, so the timing is hard to predict.

stageInfo.what: A separate WHO check of quality and manufacturing, including factory inspections. Prequalification supports eligibility for purchase under the quality assurance and procurement policies of UN agencies and major funders such as the Global Fund; specific policies and exceptions may differ. Manufacturers are invited to apply through a WHO Expression of Interest (EOI).
stageInfo.stall: Waiting for an invitation round, then for inspections.

stageInfo.what: Each country's own regulator licenses the medicine before it can be sold or used there, usually one country at a time. Regional routes, such as the African Medicines Agency and WHO's collaborative registration (about 90 working days), are intended to speed this up.
stageInfo.stall: Going country by country, each with its own queue.

stageInfo.what: Ministries of Health include the medicine in national treatment guidelines. These decide what health workers prescribe and what the public sector buys.
stageInfo.who: Ministries of Health and national malaria programmes
stageInfo.stall: National guideline committees meet rarely and follow their own schedules.

stageInfo.what: Public funders, such as the Global Fund, other donors and national governments, run tenders, agree reference prices and forecast demand. A medicine can be recommended, registered and in the guidelines and still be barely bought. This step covers public channels only: the figures shown are Global Fund-financed procurement. Private commercial channels are not included.
stageInfo.who: The Global Fund, other donors, UNICEF and national governments
stageInfo.stall: Financing cycles. Global Fund grants, for example, run for three years.
stageInfo.source: Global Fund price and quality reporting

stageInfo.what: Supply from port to health facility, health-worker training, and pharmacovigilance once the medicine is in use.
stageInfo.stall: Supply chain readiness and health-worker training.

glossary.ACT: Artemisinin-based combination therapy — the standard class of malaria treatments pairing an artemisinin derivative with a longer-acting partner drug.
glossary.SRA: Stringent Regulatory Authority — the older WHO term for an advanced regulator such as EMA or the US FDA. WHO is replacing it with WHO-Listed Authorities (WLA), regulators assessed against WHO's performance indicators; existing SRAs are treated as WHO-listed during the transition.
glossary.WLA: WHO-Listed Authority — a regulator assessed by WHO as operating at an advanced level.
glossary.EU-M4all: EU-Medicines for all, formerly the Article 58 procedure — EMA's scientific opinion on high-priority medicines intended for markets outside the EU.
glossary.GDG: Guidelines Development Group — the WHO expert group that reviews evidence and formulates treatment recommendations.
glossary.PQ: WHO prequalification — the quality, safety and efficacy assessment whose outcome, a listing on the WHO prequalified-products list, supports eligibility under the quality assurance (QA) and procurement policies of UN agencies and major funders; specific policies and exceptions may differ.
glossary.MFT: Multiple first-line therapies — the deliberate, managed use of two or more effective ACTs in a population for treatment of uncomplicated malaria, either simultaneously or in rotation.
glossary.EOI: Expression of Interest — the WHO prequalification invitation list; a product must be on it before a PQ dossier can be assessed.
glossary.AMA: African Medicines Agency — the African Union's continental medicines agency, based in Kigali, set up to harmonise regulation across the member states that have ratified its treaty and to evaluate selected priority products. National regulators still grant marketing authorisation.
glossary.PMI: U.S. President's Malaria Initiative — a major bilateral funder and procurer of malaria commodities.
glossary.MMV: Medicines for Malaria Venture — product development partnership behind several antimalarials.
glossary.PQR: Price & Quality Reporting — the Global Fund database of procurement transactions (volumes and prices).
glossary.GMP: Good Manufacturing Practice — quality standard verified by inspection of manufacturing sites.

sources.findings: Announced 12 November 2025: non-inferiority to Coartem, 97.4% PCR-corrected cure rate. This is the announcement already cited behind GanLum's R&D and regulatory stage notes; registry record is NCT05842954.
sources.relevance: Pipeline non-ACT candidate against artemisinin partial resistance; once-daily three-day granule formulation needing no separate paediatric development.

sources.label: PLOS Medicine: ASPY in routine use
sources.title: Pyronaridine-artesunate real-world safety, tolerability and effectiveness in malaria patients in 5 African countries
sources.plain: A study of how artesunate–pyronaridine performed in ordinary clinical use across five African countries.
sources.findings: Single-arm, open-label cohort event monitoring study. Published 15 June 2021 in PLOS Medicine vol. 18 — the source sheet recorded 2024 and named MMV as publisher; PLOS is the publisher and 2021 the year.
sources.relevance: Real-world safety evidence supporting adoption by national malaria control programmes and country deployment criteria.

sources.label: Rwanda: Rwanda FDA register
sources.title: Rwanda FDA register of registered pharmaceutical products
sources.plain: The national register of every medicine approved for sale in Rwanda.
sources.findings: Fetched monthly by scripts/fetch-rwanda.js. Moved by 5 Oct 2026: the old address (rwandafda.gov.rw/register/monitoring_preview_register) now redirects to www.rwandafda.gov.rw and returns 404; the register is linked as "Medicine Registers" from www.rwandafda.gov.rw/registers/products-repositories. 2,619 products on one page (7.4 MB, about 10 s); each row carries its fields as data attributes (data-regno, data-brand, data-generic, data-strength, data-mfr), which the fetcher reads. Dates are DD/MM/YYYY. Portfolio matches on 2026-10-05: DHA-PPQ x3 — DIARTEM IG ADULT 120/960mg (Rwanda FDA-HMP-MA-2273, Bliss GVS, 12 May 2025 to 11 May 2030, valid), P-ALAXIN dispersible 40/320 (MA-0903, Bliss GVS), RIDMAL 40/320 (MA-0377, Ajanta Pharma); ASPY x2 — Pyramax granules 60/20mg (MA-0182) and Pyramax tablets 180/60mg (MA-0183), both Shin Poong, 17 Aug 2024 to 16 Aug 2029. No ALAQ or GanLum, as expected.
sources.relevance: Confirms national market authorisation and commercial availability in East Africa, informing country-level procurement and deployment strategies.

sources.label: Tanzania: TMDA register
sources.title: TMDA register of medicines
sources.org: Tanzania Medicines and Medical Devices Authority
sources.plain: The national register of every medicine approved for sale in Tanzania.
sources.findings: Fetched monthly by scripts/fetch-tmda.js. 12 portfolio registrations at first snapshot, all compliant. The url changed on 12 Oct 2026: the old /portal/#/public/registered-medicines address redirects to /#/public/registered-medicines, which is now used directly.
sources.relevance: Ground truth for the country access map's registered level in Tanzania.

sources.label: Uganda: National Drug Register
sources.title: National Drug Register
sources.plain: The national register of every medicine approved for sale in Uganda.
sources.findings: Returns HTTP 403 to non-browser clients, on both the register page and the site's underlying WordPress API (checked 2026-09-21). Automation is not possible today; a person must download it. Portfolio contents not yet extracted.
sources.relevance: Authoritative national regulatory tracking for antimalarial marketing authorisations in a high-burden country.

sources.label: US President's Malaria Initiative
sources.title: US President's Malaria Initiative
sources.plain: Its public data portal closed in 2025, so US-funded purchases from that point on are a gap we cannot yet fill.
sources.findings: pmi.gov is unreachable and the USAID data hub's DNS died after the 2025 dissolution. Order-level delivery data survives only in Wayback snapshots. This is the largest disclosed coverage gap in the dashboard.
sources.relevance: Disclosing the gap is what keeps the procurement figures honest.

sources.label: Viet Nam: DAV register
sources.title: Drug Administration of Vietnam register of marketing authorisations
sources.plain: The national register of every medicine approved for sale in Viet Nam.
sources.findings: Fetched monthly by scripts/fetch-dav.js. Searched per ingredient stem; Vietnamese drops the final "e" ("Pyronaridin", "Piperaquin"). Portfolio matches on 5 Oct 2026: DHA-PPQ x10, 8 valid (including Eurartesim 20/160 and 40/320) and 2 expired; ASPY x2 — Shin Poong Pyramax. Cited on the country access map since 6 Oct 2026.
sources.relevance: Ground truth for the country access map's registered level in Viet Nam.

sources.label: WHO assessment report: DHA–PPQ (Guilin)
sources.title: WHOPAR: dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine phosphate 80mg/640mg tablets (Guilin), MA140 Part 7
sources.plain: WHO's published assessment of one prequalified dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine product.
sources.findings: Public assessment report, dated March 2026. Guilin Pharmaceutical submitted the dossier in 2017; MA140 was prequalified 2019-11-19 and already appears in our WHO PQ snapshots mapped to dhappq. WHOPAR URLs follow the pattern <ref>Part7.pdf, but not every reference has one — MA211 (prequalified Aug 2026) returns 404 — so links must be probed per product rather than assumed.
sources.relevance: Evidence of the international quality benchmark behind DHA-PPQ procurement.

sources.label: WHO assessment report: Eurartesim
sources.title: WHOPAR: Eurartesim (dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine) 20mg/160mg tablets (Alfasigma), MA093 Part 7

alsoSee.label: The same for the 40/320 mg tablet (MA094)

sources.plain: WHO's record of when Eurartesim was prequalified and when it passed its re-check.
sources.findings: MA093 Part 7, dated March 2025: "Eurartesim was listed on 09 October 2015"; requalification requested January 2024; "20 January 2025 Requirements of requalification were met. Eurartesim 160 mg/20 mg film-coated tablets remained on the list". The MA094 (40/320 mg) Part 7, dated January 2025, gives 08 January 2025 for the same step. The requalification date does not appear on the public PQ list or product pages, only in these reports.
sources.relevance: Supports Eurartesim's WHO PQ listing (9 Oct 2015) and its requalification (20 Jan 2025).

sources.label: WHO Essential Medicines List
sources.title: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 23rd list
sources.plain: WHO's list of the medicines every health system should be able to supply.
sources.findings: This URL is the 23rd list (2023). A 2025 Model List has since been published and is what the electronic EML now serves, so citing the 2023 edition means citing a superseded list — confirm which edition should be carried. No public API; export by hand per release (biennial, next revision 2027). Licence is CC BY 3.0 IGO, with no non-commercial clause.
sources.relevance: Listing supports drug rotation policies that delay resistance to dominant artemether-lumefantrine.

sources.label: WHO malaria guidelines
sources.title: WHO Guidelines for Malaria
sources.plain: Which medicines the World Health Organization recommends, and from when.
sources.findings: Living guideline, revised one to three times a year, so a fixed publication year goes stale silently. Current version confirmed 2026-09-21 via the MAGICapp API (guideline 10462): "WHO guidelines for malaria - 13 August 2025", last edited 2 September 2025. That API is free and needs no key, so a version watcher is buildable and is not yet built.
sources.relevance: The gate every product passes at the WHO recommendation stage; DHA-PPQ is recommended first- and second-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum with long post-treatment prophylaxis.

sources.label: WHO Malaria Threats Map
sources.title: WHO Malaria Threats Map
sources.org: WHO Department of Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases (MNT)

alsoSee.label: The same study results as a searchable database

sources.year: Continuous; major refresh around the World Malaria Report
sources.plain: Where malaria is becoming harder to treat. Its drug-resistance study results are not reproduced on this page — open the map to explore them.
sources.findings: Until 1 Oct 2026 its therapeutic efficacy study (TES) and molecular-marker extracts fed the map's resistance layers (data/resistance.js, data/molecular-markers.js); those layers were removed and the page now links here instead. The antimalarial drug efficacy database under alsoSee is the same data with a different front door — it is not a second source. The ArcGIS service underneath both is documented as unstable; do not build automation on it.
sources.relevance: Tracks PCR-corrected cure rates and molecular resistance markers, including plasmepsin 2/3 duplications; underpins treatment policy transitions.

sources.label: WHO malaria treatment guidelines, 2010
sources.title: Guidelines for the treatment of malaria, 2nd edition
sources.plain: WHO's 2010 treatment guidelines, which first recommended DHA–PPQ.
sources.findings: WHO IRIS record 10665/44227: 'Guidelines for the treatment of malaria', 2nd ed, ISBN 9789241547925, issued 2010, xi + 194 pp. (the IRIS page renders in a browser; metadata checked via the IRIS API). Box 2, 'Additional recommendations in the second edition of the Guidelines (2010)': "Dihydroartemisinin plus piperaquine (DHA+PPQ) is an option for the first-line treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria worldwide. Strong recommendation, high quality evidence." Section 7 lists five recommended ACTs, the fifth being DHA+PPQ, and notes no DHA+PPQ product was yet prequalified or SRA-registered. www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241547925 returns 404. No WHO news item of 10 Dec 2010 was found; one secondary slide deck gives the 2nd edition's release date as 9 March 2010 (not verified).
sources.relevance: Supports DHA-PPQ's WHO recommendation in 2010 as the fifth ACT.

sources.label: WHO MFT implementation guide
sources.title: Multiple first-line therapies as part of the response to antimalarial drug resistance: an implementation guide
sources.org: World Health Organization, Department of Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases (MNT)
sources.plain: WHO's guide to using several first-line malaria treatments at once, with country examples.
sources.findings: Annex 2 (pp. 21-22) gives country plans. Nigeria: a pilot is planned in two areas, with 20% AL, 40% DHA-PPQ and 40% ASPY where seasonal malaria chemoprevention runs, and 10% ASAQ, 20% AL, 35% DHA-PPQ and 35% ASPY elsewhere. Rwanda: AL, DHA-PPQ and ASPY in rotation in six pilot districts, 2024-2025. Uganda: rotation only "being considered". Tanzania: scope "remains to be confirmed"; the guide says ASPY was not yet registered there, which TMDA's own register contradicts (Pyramax since 2017). Cited on the country access map since 6 Oct 2026. The url changed on 12 Oct 2026: it was the IRIS PDF download; it is now WHO's publication page, and the PDF is an alsoSee link.
sources.relevance: Supports the In MFT plans level for Nigeria (planned) and Rwanda.

sources.label: WHO national drug policy table
sources.title: World Malaria Report 2025, Annex 4B: Antimalarial drug policy in malaria endemic countries and areas, 2024
sources.plain: Which malaria medicines each country's national treatment policy lists, and for which patients.
sources.findings: Downloaded by hand once a year and normalised by scripts/normalize-treatment-policy.js into data/treatment-policy.js, which drives the Show MFT policy switch on the country access map. Re-checked 5 Oct 2026: all 15 countries listing ASPY or DHA-PPQ match the raw annex in sourcing/raw/wmr/. It describes 2024 and lags national changes: it lists no ASPY for Ghana (first-line since 2022, frontiers-ghana-tes), AL only for Rwanda (its 2024 guidelines list DHA-PPQ and ASPY), and neither medicine for Kenya.
sources.relevance: WHO's own country-by-country record of national treatment policy; the source for the map's national guidelines level.

sources.label: WHO PQ comparator products
sources.title: Recommended comparator products: antimalarial medicines
sources.plain: The reference products a generic must be tested against before WHO will list it.
sources.findings: Names the reference products used in antimalarial bioequivalence work. Not a list of prequalified formulations, and not product-specific to any one medicine in the portfolio.
sources.relevance: Establishes the reference standard for generic bioequivalence studies, enabling generic market entry and competitive pricing.

sources.label: WHO PQ: 24th malaria EOI invitation, 2025
sources.title: 24th Invitation to Manufacturers of Antimalarial Medicines to Submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) for Product Evaluation to the WHO Prequalification Unit (PQT)
sources.plain: The list of malaria medicines WHO currently invites manufacturers to submit for prequalification.
sources.findings: WHO PQ news item dated 27 February 2026 says the invitation "was recently updated. It now includes Artemether/Lumefantrine, dispersible tablet 5 mg/60 mg (as an additional strength) under point 2." The linked PDF (EOI-MalariaV24_2.pdf) is headed '24th Invitation' and dated 19 November 2025. Its fixed-dose ACT lists cover AL, AS-AQ, AS-MQ, artesunate-pyronaridine (tablet 60/180, granules 20/60) and DHA-PPQ (60/480, 80/640; paediatric 20/160, 30/240, 40/320). It contains no ganaplacide-lumefantrine and no artemether-lumefantrine-amodiaquine. So '27 Feb 2026' is the date of the update notice, not of the document; '24th malaria EOI, updated 27 Feb 2026' is the accurate wording.
sources.relevance: Supports 'not on the WHO PQ EOI list yet' for GanLum and ALAQ.

sources.label: WHO prequalification guidance
sources.title: WHO medicines prequalification guidance
sources.plain: WHO's rules for how a medicine gets prequalified.
sources.findings: Process guidance, not data. In the source sheet this row carried the comparator list's title; the two are different documents and are separated here.
sources.relevance: Sets out the quality benchmark manufacturers must meet to enter donor-funded supply chains.

sources.label: WHO prequalification list
sources.title: WHO list of prequalified finished pharmaceutical products

alsoSee.label: Prevention tools are on a separate list

sources.plain: The medicines WHO has checked for quality, safety and effectiveness.
sources.findings: Fetched monthly by scripts/fetch-regulatory.js. CSV headers drift between editions; suspensions and delistings are published as separate notices, so the pipeline snapshots and diffs rather than trusting the current file.
sources.relevance: Quality-assured supply is a precondition for donor procurement.

sources.label: WHO: child malaria medicine priorities, 2025
sources.title: Paediatric drug optimization for malaria: meeting report, 24-26 June 2025
sources.plain: WHO's list of child-friendly malaria medicines that most need developing, from a June 2025 meeting.
sources.findings: WHO publication page dated 14 November 2025 (meeting 24-26 June 2025; ISBN 978-92-4-011698-6, 30 pp.). The Group "decided to include artemether-lumefantrine-amodiaquine in the PADO priority list as 20/120/40 mg taste-masked dispersible tablets". Table 3, 'Antimalarial candidates discussed by the PADO-malaria Group, which have not yet been reviewed by WHO for guidelines', lists artemether + lumefantrine + amodiaquine and ganaplacide-lumefantrine. Artesunate-pyronaridine granules 20 mg + 60 mg are on its access list. It says nothing about EOI listing or PQ timing for ALAQ. It confirms the 'taste-masked' wording that the 23 Aug 2026 changelog removed as unverified.
sources.relevance: Supports ALAQ's child-friendly formulation and that neither ALAQ nor GanLum has yet been reviewed for WHO guidelines.

sources.label: WWARN / IDDO malaria data
sources.title: WWARN / IDDO malaria data repository
sources.org: WorldWide Antimalarial Resistance Network / Infectious Diseases Data Observatory
sources.plain: Pooled results from many separate studies of how well antimalarials still work.
sources.findings: Curated repository of standardised individual patient clinical and molecular data. Only published aggregates are usable to us: patient-level data sits behind IDDO's Data Access Committee under a data use agreement and cannot be redistributed. Literature-derived, so it overlaps who-threat-maps — neither is a superset of the other.
sources.relevance: Informs resistance mitigation investment, dose optimisation and policy transitions through pooled efficacy evidence.

sources.label: Zambia: ZAMRA register
sources.title: ZAMRA register of human medicines
sources.plain: The national register of every medicine approved for sale in Zambia.
sources.findings: Fetched monthly by scripts/fetch-zamra.js. The whole register in one call (3,519 medicines on 5 Oct 2026). Its server omits an intermediate certificate, which is supplied from scripts/certs/ with verification left on. Portfolio matches on 5 Oct 2026: ASPY x1 — Pyramax tablets, ZAMRA-HM-25-239, 11 Jul 2025 to 10 Jul 2030, Registered/Compliant; DHA-PPQ x7. Cited on the country access map since 6 Oct 2026. The url changed on 12 Oct 2026: it was the fetcher's data address, which shows an SQL error in a browser; it is now the public register page, and the data address is dataUrl.
sources.relevance: Ground truth for the country access map's registered level in Zambia.

sources.findings: Fetched monthly by scripts/fetch-mcaz.js. The whole register in one request (3,154 medicines on 5 Oct 2026). Portfolio matches on 5 Oct 2026: DHA-PPQ x1 — DUO-COTECXIN 40/320mg, 2025/7.5/7111, 27 Oct 2025 to 26 Oct 2030. No ASPY. Cited on the country access map since 6 Oct 2026.
sources.relevance: Ground truth for the country access map's registered level in Zimbabwe.
